title: Weighing the Evidence
sub: Grades 5–8 ELA · Our Incredible Moon · Claim, counterclaim and evidence
objective: Students will read the poster’s paragraph about Apollo 11 as a short argument: a claim, a counterclaim it answers, evidence, and a conclusion. They will weigh each piece of evidence, including the panels the exhibition adds beside it, and write their own claim, evidence and reasoning paragraph. At Red, they will set the poster’s argument beside an idea it calls a *theory* that the exhibition’s own note calls an untested hypothesis.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every day we meet surprising claims. Knowing how to weigh evidence, and how to answer someone who doubts, is how a careful reader decides what to believe.

items.text: find the claim, the counterclaim, the evidence and the conclusion in a short argument

materials: Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed: the paragraph as it appears on the poster
Highlighters in two colors (Yellow and Red levels); differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **On the poster** *Our Incredible Moon*, find the paragraph beginning *In 1969* and the panels beside it: the samples, the prisms and the photographs of the landing sites. On *Another Earth*, find the Dark Forest paragraph and the note beneath it.

steps.title: “The Eagle has landed.”
script: Play the recording of July 20, 1969: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the Sea of Tranquility while Michael Collins circled the Moon. Then ask: *“How do we know this really happened?”* Take answers without judging. Some students may have heard people say it did not. *“Today we read how the poster answers them, and decide whether its answer is strong.”*

steps.title: Claim and counterclaim
script: **Claim and counterclaim.** Read the paragraph’s opening. The **claim**: humans landed on the Moon in 1969, and there is strong evidence. The **counterclaim**, the view it answers: *“Some people have questioned whether the Moon landings were real.”* Notice *but*: it turns from the doubt to the answer.

screen.text: In 1969, humans achieved the remarkable feat of landing on the Moon during NASA’s Apollo 11 mission. Some people have questioned whether the Moon landings were real, but there’s strong evidence proving this happened.

steps.purpose: Find the claim, and the counterclaim it answers.
students: What does the writer want us to believe?
Whose view does the writer answer?

steps.title: The evidence
script: **Evidence and conclusion.** *For example* and *Additionally* signal two pieces of **evidence**: the Moon rocks, unlike any on Earth, and the tracking by scientists around the world. *All this evidence confirms* signals the **conclusion**.

screen.text: For example, the astronauts brought back Moon rocks that are very different from any rocks found on Earth. These rocks have unique features that couldn’t be faked or created on our planet. Additionally, the missions were tracked by scientists around the world. All this evidence confirms that humans truly did land on the Moon in 1969.

steps.purpose: Find the evidence and the conclusion.
students: What two pieces of evidence are given?
Which words signal evidence? Which signal the conclusion?

steps.title: Strong or weak?
script: **Weigh it.** The exhibition adds panels beside the paragraph: *“Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo missions brought back 842 pounds (382 kilograms) of Moon rocks, pebbles, sand, and dust: 2,200 separate samples in all. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon.”* And: *“Apollo 11 left a panel of 100 small glass prisms on the Moon. Scientists still fire lasers at it today and time the light’s trip back, to measure the distance to the Moon to within a few millimeters. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has also photographed all six Apollo landing sites from above, where the landers and even the astronauts’ boot tracks can be seen.”* Fill in the chart together. Strong evidence can be checked by others, especially today, and does not depend on trusting one person. Ask: is the poster’s paragraph stronger with the panels, or without them?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three take the poster’s argument apart and end with a paragraph of their own.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Sort five sentences from the poster into claim, counterclaim, evidence and conclusion. Pick the two strongest pieces of evidence. Write a paragraph with a sentence frame.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Rank five pieces of evidence and explain each choice. Write a paragraph that states a claim, uses two pieces of evidence and answers the counterclaim.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Judge which evidence could be checked today. Compare the Apollo argument with the *Dark Forest* idea and the note beside it. Write an argument that answers the doubters fairly.

steps.purpose: Take an argument apart and write one, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three end with a paragraph of your own.

steps.title: Surprising claims
script: Close with the poster’s own question, on the screen. Two or three students share; listen for *checked by others* and *can be checked today*.

screen.question: Some people have questioned whether the Moon landings were real. When you hear a surprising claim, what kinds of evidence would help you decide whether to believe it?

steps.purpose: Carry the lesson beyond the Moon: how to weigh any surprising claim.
students: Think of a surprising claim you have heard.
What evidence would change your mind?
